title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
purpose: It presents a dialogue-form treatise in which a jurist defends the adhan formula 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of human beings, and their kindred are the best of kindred' with eight Quranic proofs, then rebuts objections concerning addition to and subtraction from the call to prayer.

points.text: The section is framed as a recorded debate: one jurist challenges another over why his school alone says in the call to prayer 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of human beings, and their kindred are the best of kindred,' and the respondent undertakes to answer.

The respondent's first reply is that by Quran 41:46 and 6:164 the formula, if righteous, benefits only its users and, if wrong, harms only them, so no other group is burdened by it — a reply the questioner accepts while still demanding a plain proof.

The questioner concedes as established that Muhammad is the best of human beings because he is master of the messengers, but denies that Ali's likeness to him in that excellence is established, and demands proof — so only Ali's rank is actually in dispute.

Proof one argues from the Purification verse (33:33) that the people of the household are equal to the Prophet in purity, and since Ali is the most excellent of them and the Prophet's guardian and successor, likeness to the Prophet is established for him.

Proofs two, three and six argue from 'Peace be upon the family of Yasin' (37:130), 'You are the best community brought forth for humankind' (3:110), and 'those who believe and do righteous deeds are the best of creation' (98:7) that these verses address the Prophet's household, and since Ali is first and most excellent among them he is the best of human beings.

Proof four reasons that God granted Moses's request for Aaron as minister, brother, sharer in his task and holder of joint authority, and that since God's way admits no change or alteration (35:43, 17:77) and Muhammad was told to follow earlier prophets' guidance, Muhammad was obliged to appoint Ali in the same role — confirmed by the hadith 'Ali stands to me in the station of Aaron to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me.'

Proof five argues from the Guardianship verse (5:55–56), read as revealed concerning Ali, that he shares with the Messenger guardianship over the believers, a station only the best of human beings after the Messenger could hold — reinforced by the Prophet's declaration at Ghadir Khumm, 'Whoever's master I am, this Ali is his master.'

Proofs seven and eight argue from 3:33–34 (God chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of Imran) and 44:30–32 (God chose the Children of Israel above the worlds) that, since Muhammad is more excellent than all prophets, his family surpasses the family of every prophet in every era, and Ali is the most excellent of that family.

An objection is reported from opponents of the school: that Umar's removal of 'Hayya ala khayr al-amal' from the adhan is unproven from their books, was in any case a sound exercise of judgment, and that if it were an error then adding 'I testify that our master Ali is the guardian of God' would equally be an error, since adder and subtractor are alike.
entities: Ashhadu anna mawlana Aliyyan waliyy Allah

points.text: The author replies that even conceding both addition and subtraction to be error, the two are not of equal degree, for four reasons: the subtractor misled vastly more people; he preceded al-Hakim by over four centuries and the earlier misleader is more culpable; he not only subtracted but added the ugly sentence 'prayer is better than sleep,' setting prayer against sleep as though comparing a sword to wood; and he dropped the Prophet's phrase from all five prayers while attaching his own only to the dawn prayer.

The author rejects as void slander the ascription of the guardianship phrase to al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, noting that the Twelver Shia, though differing from him in school, also use it in the call to prayer.

Against the claim that Umar's subtraction is absent from the opponents' books, the author answers that the disputed soundness and fabricated reports of Sahih al-Bukhari, the other five, and al-Mishkat relieve the people of truth of any need to refute them, and that al-Qadi al-Numan's narration from Jafar al-Sadiq predates those compilations, which may well have suppressed the report to avoid censure.

On the origin of the added phrase, the author holds that the testimony to guardianship issued from Ali himself about himself once the office passed to him after the Prophet, just as the Prophet testified to his own prophethood and God testified concerning His own oneness (3:18).
